utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you are to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Tabeau. We shall pick up on where we left off yesterday. Let me remind you of your last answer to the question I put to you. "What difference is there between conflict statistical method and official statistical method." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I noticed that in your work, you didn't indicate why you had chosen this method, i.e., statistics related to conflict. Could you tell us why you chose this method in particular?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, for this particular report, well, I think that I didn't have really much choice. This is a conflict situation that we talk about; and as in every conflict, also in the Sarajevo conflict, sources on the casualties of this conflict were limited and in many ways deficient. So it was not really possible to apply the usual statistical approach or usual approach. With good sources, systematic registration of all deaths or wounding persons, it was not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, your best source according to what have you said in your expert report, you have used the data stemming from two official demographic institutes; one in the Republika Srpska and the other in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Federation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. On reading your report, I realised that when you mentioned the most reliable source, for the most part, you used death certificate excerpts, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understand the question; but if you are you saying that the two largest sources, RS database and FBiH database, were established using documentation such as including death certificates, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I realised on reading your report. Is that a standard procedure that is used when determining the death rate in a particular country?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The death rate is obtained based on vital events registration data. This is the death registration data. This is similar to the databases that I used for this report, and this registration is indeed based on death certification. That is very correct. The difference is that the databases I used, I know and the statistical authority who is established them know these databases are incomplete, and there are certain deficiencies that normally wouldn't be there in normal times, in a time of peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us what these deficiencies were and why you chose the conflicts statistical method, in addition to the fact that you had, according to what you said, fairly reliable statistical databases?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I don't want that an impression would prevail here that there are different statistical methods that are used in official statistics and that are used in conflict research. The methods are just statistical methods. What is really different is the availability of information. I'm speaking of sources. We don't have the same sources for conflict situations. We don't have the same sources as normally in the time of peace. So the methods are all the time, always. The way we apply them must be different because of the sources. What was the other part of your question? The deficiencies of your the sources. So the first and most probably meaningful is that the registration is incomplete, and that it is incomplete is pretty certain. This is related, on one hand, to the fact that during the conflict situation the statistical authority was unable to function normally. There was a chaotic situation and not all reports were received in time and registered in time. And, secondly, and very importantly, there were massive migration movements in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the conflict already, starting from the beginning of the conflict. At the end of the conflict, about 50 per cent of the population changed their place of residence. So that would be more than 2 million people who didn't live anymore at the same residence as before the war. Partly, these were internally displaced persons; partly these were people who migrated out of Bosnia-Herzegovina due to conflict reasons. So these huge population movements implied that there were difficulties, that families could actually -- were not really able to report that to the proper authorities in time. So that is the incompleteness. There were also other deficiencies, like, for instance, the required death certificate was not always available for every record. Death certificates were attached to about 75 per cent of records registered in databases on average. I'm not speaking of concrete numbers. It's the level generally. And, of course, the reporting wasn't perfect because it was often done in traumatic situations, so certain details, like, for instance, dates, were incomplete or misreported or places were misspelled, names were misspelled. Those kind of deficiencies can be seen in these databases.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, other witnesses have shown before this Chamber that the territory controlled by Bosnia-Herzegovina updated all their records. I'm talking about status of various individuals. We've seen forensic reports here establishing accidental deaths, violent accidental deaths. You haven't used these sources, have you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what kind of sources are you talking about. You are speaking of forensic reports by Bosnian authorities. If you could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that yesterday Judge Harhoff put this question to you. And you answered by saying that the dead people don't -- are not admitted into evidence hospital and, therefore, are not listed on the hospital lists. We have here another proof of the fact that the dead for the most part - I can't say whether this was the case at all times - but that it was a forensic medic who registered the deaths, like in all normal countries. But you did not use this database to prepare your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to that question on the grounds that it is vague. Counsel has not specified what database she is talking. She's talking about people not being admitted into hospitals who are dead, but I'm not sure -- I at least am completely in the dark as to what database the witness is being asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What database do you have in mind, Ms. Isailovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I mean are the death registers in the hospitals of Sarajevo. This evidence was presented before this Chamber. It was the Prosecutor who adduced this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know this -- I wanted to know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's ask the witness. Yes. You're being asked, Mrs. Tabeau, whether you availed yourself of the information from the registration of deaths in hospitals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we discussed this issue shortly yesterday; and I said that from hospitals, information would be available about this persons who died in hospital of their wounds. And I did not use this information. That, actually, is available to me. This is a very small number of records, as these are records related only to the small sample of people wounded and related to the indictment period. We are speaking of the wounded persons who were 405, for whom I have extensive documentation. So for those of them who died, there is, in addition, a record of death from hospitals. But generally people who died on streets are generally not in hospitals. These people were not brought to hospital in order to issue death certificate for them. This is not the general practice in death registration. The family has the obligation to notify statistical authority about the death, and this needs to be done based on a death certificate that normally is issued by a physician or another qualified person, say, medically trained person, and this arranged, I guess, by authorities together with the family, right? But this is not that every death normally has to be reported to hospital in order to be registered.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we shouldn't confuse matters. I heard that you mentioned 405 cases that have been recorded by the hospital; but on reading your report, I believe that this figure related to the number of wounded, i.e., 405. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 405 are indeed wounded persons. The small sample of wounded persons who were in hospitals, we have for these persons also, for those who died of their wounds, information about death from the hospital. But this is a very small group of individuals. I think, in general terms, if one would like -- sorry, this last part is to be neglected, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: My next question runs as follows: Where did you get this information? The fact that people were dying on the streets, or that people were not admitted into hospital or not brought by policemen into hospital?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did I get the information that people were dying on streets. I think, well, if this information is indeed not listed directly in the databases that I used, well, we -- seeing the places they were dying at, of course, the streets are mentioned. All kinds of places are mentioned as the place of death. So it is pretty sure that they were dying at all kind of places, on streets, in their apartments, in trams, and in cars, yeah, in the river. They were dying everywhere. This is one thing. Well, whether they were not admitted into hospital, if they had been admitted, all of them, to hospital, then I believe that there would be a record of these, available from the hospitals. I probably need to explain a little bit about the project related to hospital records. The OTP ran this project in 1997 with the purpose of actually collecting all available information from hospitals about wounded persons, persons wounded during the conflict. So a group of investigators, OTP investigators, visited three major hospitals in Sarajevo; Kosevo, State, and Dobrinja. They arrange at the hospitals that the staff would extract from their archives all existing files of patients admitted to these hospitals during the conflict. Generally, there were thousands of files available at the hospitals, but the OTP was interested only in those files that were related to patients that were wounded by shelling, sniping, or other fire-arms in conflict situation. The files that the OTP wanted were of the civilians. These, of course, had to define who is a civilian without knowing the circumstances in which the person was wounded. So the general principle here applied to us that all files selected were of women; and if the files were of men, then an age was required to be below 18 or above 60. So the men at the military ages, active military ages were exclude from this selection. As a result of this project, a little bit more than 3.000 files were extracted from the three major hospitals related to the entire conflict, that means April 1992 until November -- December of 1995. Of those approximately 3.000 files, a small sample, 405 cases, individuals, I extracted as relevant to this indictment. This is how we obtained this documentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, I shall get back to what I mentioned beforehand. You did not use the hospital records established by medical examiners. You only checked these records for the purpose of establishing how many wounded people there were.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I disagree, and strongly, because I used the death certificates. I used the death certificates. Those are the documents that are issued by medical examiners in the case of death. I use them because these are the two largest databases that I used; FBiH and RS databases. These databases as the underlying documentation have the death certificates and other documents declaring a person dead. So I strongly disagree. I did use the death certificate, but I didn't use the death report from hospital, that report from the hospital, because there was no need to do so. Why was -- I can even explain why there was no need to do so. I believe that the death certificates used by statistical authorities in both political entities partly, most likely, came from the hospitals as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You will understand why I'm putting all these questions to you. In conflict statistics, you use what is called extrapolation, I believe. This is a standard method in a conflict situation when there are no 100 per cent reliable sources to determine how many dead people there are. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used extrapolation in order to improve the statistics related to the wounded persons. I didn't use the extrapolation in relation to the killed persons. I produced statistics on the killed that came from the counting approach. Counting is actual counting, yes, looking for all these individuals and just adding them up to together. This is the counting approach.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you matched the data from your sources to establish how many dead people there were. Let's look at these in a moment. These are the charts in which you give us the figures from your sources, and then you use an adjustment method which is used in conflict statistics, where you use a hypothesis to establish what has happened rather than bearing in mind the real situation?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you are speaking of the two types of minimum numbers that I presented on the killed; the absolute minimum and the adjusted more likely minimum. It was minimum, of course, in both cases. In the second case, I indeed made an adjustment. That means, yeah, some kind of extrapolation combined with the counting approach figure, I presented the more likely number. I don't think it is a wrong approach. It is a method that is often used; not only in conflict demography, but also in historical demography. This method is very popular, and I think it has a very strong statistical foundation which discussed in the annex. It is just a standard statistical standard to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, I would like you to confirm that the specific difference between the two statistical methods is that in the conflict statistical method you use this method, whereby, you provide an explanation for things you don't know so much about because you don't have 100 per cent reliable sources; whereas, in a demographical statistical method, you established what is true because you base this on accurate records. This is the main difference between these two methods, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are speaking about the explanation. This is not what I did in this report. I didn't explain anything. I just presented statistics that are measures of victimisation, expressed in terms of the killed and wounded persons. Well, measures can be produced as figures obtained from the counting approach or measure can be obtained as estimates. Estimates are statistical visions of certain indicators. Estimates, however, even though they don't rely on counting, rely on, in some part, on observed, existing, available data, and, in part, on certain assumptions that we apply to the data that is available. And I think that both figures obtained from counting and figures obtained as estimates are frequently used in conflict research and at the same time in normal demography and official statistics. Well, if you think, for instance, about pensions, the pension system is based on estimates of life expectancy. This is not observed as a figure obtained from a counting approach. It is an estimate, especially if you think of models that are made to establish budgets for every state. So this is all based on estimates. It is not observed numbers that are used for it. But it is still the best we can do it is as close to the truth as we can get.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Mrs. Tabeau. You used this method based on estimates, didn't you, in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used both. I used counting approach and I used estimation as well. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: My last question on these sources which you did not use: Bosnian police provides records of all incidents having occurred according to their interpretation, stemming from snipers or shells and coming from the Republika Srpska. We've had complete data from the police. Now, as far as the area of Sarajevo controlled by Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, were you aware of the existence of such records?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether I was aware of the existence, yes, I was. I knew that such records were collected by the OTP, and I knew that OTP, the Prosecution team was busy with establishing a database with these records. I would be very happy to be able to analyse this data, but this was not possible for various reasons. That's all I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And why wasn't it possible?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly because of time restriction. I actually was very eager to get my hands on this data, but there was a lot of time pressure and deadlines, short deadlines for finishing this report. This is the only reason, the major reason, that I didn't use them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The answer you provided; namely, that you had time constraints, you realise that the indictment goes back to 1998, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But do you realise on how many cases I have worked on in this Tribunal. It is not the only case I have been working on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, the police records which provided details on the number of injured, the number of dead people supposedly from where the army of Republika Srpska was quartered, would this be high quality sources to things which you could use; namely, establish whether violent deaths was due to the war or not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know the data, and I don't know this source particularly well, but I do have some impression of this data, for many incidents, victims were reported in terms of aggregate statistics; numbers were available, no names, and no other personal details. From the point of view of the work we have done in this report, it is a serious deficiency that wouldn't be possible. Exactly the same thing present as this report wouldn't be possible for this data. But I believe that studying the data on incidents, be it sniping, shelling, both, would be a very valuable addition to the statistics presented in this report. Why? It is yet another source on practically the same victims, so it would certainly give additional insights into what we were able to present in our report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: The evidence the Chamber has heard until now demonstrates that in all police records on the -- in the area of Sarajevo controlled by Bosnia-Herzegovina had names, first names, surnames, and dates of birth of a number of people. Would this have been a quality source for you or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I believe that misstates the evidence. The evidence is that the records selected for the spreadsheet that was introduced into evidence last week had to have certain data in them in order to be selected, and I believe that the next witness will have further evidence regarding those criteria, but I don't think it is correct to state that every police record will contain a name, a date of birth, and so forth. I don't think there is evidence of that in the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And as far as I remember, I also stressed that certain records didn't include personal information of victims, and I didn't say that all these records on incidents didn't have information about victims. If we can go back to the transcript, we can check this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, take that into consideration, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I must say that I have understood nothing. I didn't understand the objection made by Mr. Docherty. I didn't have time to look at the transcript. What statement are we talking about here? I honestly don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand the objection was to the formulation of your question along the lines that the records in the area of Sarajevo had names, first names, surnames, and dates of birth of a number of people, and you asked the witness whether this will have been a quality source. Mr. Docherty said that the evidence did not show that the records had each and every item that you referred to, and the witness has confirmed that. So perhaps you should just reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I have understood you correctly, Mr. Docherty has challenged the quality of his own evidence. I haven't quite understood. Did Mr. Docherty say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. What he has said is that you formulated a question on the basis of the evidence and that you misstated the evidence because you suggested to the witness that the evidence that she gave was that the records had certain data, names, et cetera, and she did not say that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I say something, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, there are two things. There was this selection of records submitted by the Prosecution. There is a more extensive record of these incidents, as far as I understand. And the selection most likely, I don't know the selection, but the selection most likely included a lot of personal information, the selection submitted by the Prosecution. But I know the broader picture of these data, and I know that there are various types of records in -- from this source. Some are very general, like reporting only the numbers of victims without personal details about individuals. But there are others, very good records with very, very broad information about victims as well. But generally it is not true that we, for all the records, don't have names and other personal information. That is not true. For some we have, and for some we don't. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that's the position. For some the data, the personal data is available; for others the data is not available.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now get back to the sources that you have used and the Sarajevo Ten and Sarajevo Six samples. First of all, you used the data provided by the Statistical Institute of Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina. The data were updated at the request of the OTP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The databases were established on request of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So after that, you then matched these two databases, and you came up with a database that contained, on the one hand, the Republika Srpska Statistical Institute data and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina authority databases?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point, yes, indeed, we merged these two databases. We did it because the coverage of these two databases is largely exclusive. So Republika Srpska is related to the territory of the Republika Srpska; and FBiH database, the territory of the Federation. But there is a small overlap as well. Certain records are reported in both; not many.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that among the instructions provided to both institutes was that the name of the municipality in which the death had occurred had to be mentioned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't provide instructions of -- on details. We generally requested that the documentation, death documentation available to the authorities, documentation covering the conflict period in Bosnia and Herzegovina, be computerised. They themselves, the statistical authority, decided on how they would do it. They applied, each authority, the standard statistical approach, including the standard death notification form for reporting of the death. But, indeed, municipality of death is one of the items in this form as a standard item always provided to the statistical authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, in order to establish your two samples, Sarajevo Ten and Sarajevo Six, you needed to have that information, i.e., the name of the municipality. That was a prerequisite, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand the question. We used the municipalities as officially -- as official administrative units. We used the pre-war municipalities as basis for the death registration. This is the approach the statistical authority followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: This has been mentioned already. In your database in which you collected data from the two statistical institutes, you had the death records which provided the name of the municipalities in question, which enabled you to come up with your sample, Sarajevo Six and Sarajevo Ten. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is generally the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Once you had collected all this data in Stari Grad, Ilidza, who provided the municipality break down? Was this done with a computer or were the data already contained in your statistical data?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was no break down at all. It is the pre-war municipalities of Sarajevo for which statistics are given.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] -- breakdown for distribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We had last the interpretation for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: -- breakdown for distribution. Once you had prepared your database stemming from the two statistical institutes A, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, B, from Republika Srpska. Now, to break down the data, according to each municipality, someone had to divide it between these two municipalities or break it down according to each municipality. Was this done with a computer or not? Because the name of the municipality was already provided on the statistical data sheet, and this was in the computer.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of municipalities were reported on the death notification forms and were entered into computer by the staff of the statistical authorities that were establishing the databases. I can even give you more detail, that for the municipalities a standardized list was used with coding usually applied to municipalities by the statistical authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I will now give you a sample. Let's take the case, for instance, of the municipality of Ilidza. It is mentioned in your Sarajevo Six sample, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, the two statistical bodies already had that data regarding Ilidza as being a neighbourhood of Sarajevo. According to them, this -- these were part of the Ilidza municipality?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand the question well. I think that -- I don't see a problem. I don't see an issue, so this is -- I don't know what it is about. If you could rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I can. Well, let's take the example of Ilidza municipality. That municipality belonged to its territory both for Republika Srpska and the BiH federation. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The new municipal division of Bosnia-Herzegovina that was introduced after the Dayton peace agreement split a number of municipalities into two parts; one part belonging to one political entity, one belonging to the other political entity. Several of Sarajevo municipalities actually were split as well. But this is not an issue in this project. The municipalities were reported by respective statistical authorities in terms of pre-war municipalities. The post-war municipalities were smaller than the pre-war municipalities, but they added up the records provided to cover the entire municipality. This is not an issue that would produce any bias in statistics at all. Why? Because the basis for our calculations are individual records, individual cases, persons. Duplicates are searched for using personal information. So if there were records overlapping for municipalities like Ilidza reported by one and the second authority, we were able to exclude the duplicated record using the searches based on personal information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Tabeau, you said for the statistics, the death certificates that were issued when death occurred were used, did you not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. But name is part of the death certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, as well as the municipality where death occurred, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right, most likely. I note that I have a death certificate in front of me right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And because these two -- I do not know how to refer to them, because we're talking about civil authorities during the war with one reporting to the BiH government and the other reporting to the Republika Srpska government. So both of these institutions issued death certificates with names of municipalities which naturally were not different from one another because for the BiH government Hrasnica was Ilidza --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have now got your point. These databases were established of the material that comes from the conflict period. Normally, there are local vital events registration offices, local, not municipality, just local offices. Population living in an area, in the case of death of a family member, has to notify this local statistical authority of the death. So the documentation comes from the conflict period from all local authorities spread all over the country. The federal and arrest statistical authority, the offices in Banja Luka and in Sarajevo, made an effort and centralised these documentation. They physically collected the documentation from the local offices to the central office; and then based on this documentation, they completed this project for us. So it is not that the statistical authority of federation or RS were collected death certificates. Not at all. The documentation existed already long before this project -- project were completed by the authorities. So it was a process that was taking place, the documentation I mean, of issuing the death certificates and registration. Death registration was a process that took place in the conflict period. The statistical authority collected kind of retrospectively the available documentation and computerised data. So the reporting of the municipalities was according to the available standards at the time, and the new municipalities were introduced after the Dayton agreement which is after the conflict. So we have no issue of new versus old municipalities here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Tabeau, let me put you an example of things to be as simple as possible. In your sample, Sarajevo Six, say, for example, the Ilidza municipality, but this would be valid for other municipalities, but I'm picking this one. So as far as that is concerned, you are saying that you blame the accused for all accidental deaths occurring in Ilidza during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Objection. That statement is argumentative and it completely misstates the evidence. The witness has not said that she blames anything for these deaths. She has simply stated that she collected death statistics. I believe the question should be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or reformulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not know how to rephrase this. Maybe I could use the conditional tense, because yesterday we discussed this when discussing the statistical conclusions of the report. As regards the Sarajevo Six and the time covered by the indictment, and Mr. Docherty said this was the right question to ask, he said that the number of victims is going to be very high and will be relevant when sentencing the accused. I'm not inventing or making anything up. What I'm saying is we're talking about Sarajevo Six and the indictment period, and we're talking about all the deaths. So I don't know how to phrase it differently. But at the end of the day, all the deaths will be attributed to the accused. There is just an observation and then I will move on to my question, if I may. I'm not saying that the witness is accusing anyone, but --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, that is a submission which the Prosecution may make in its closing arguments, but to say that the witness is blaming the accused for all accidental deaths occurring in Ilidza is not correct. If you wish, you can reformulate the question; if you can't, then move on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not know how to phrase things differently because you can look at this sample, and perhaps I could did the question differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Move on to another matter. If you can't put the question in a form that is permissible, please move on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. For the purposes of your expert report, have you counted all the deaths in Ilidza in your Sarajevo Six sample during the indictment period, indictment against Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I included the entire Ilidza in the statistics. Well, I think we agreed yesterday, as well, that the report is made from the end of deaths, not incidents. I didn't use the data on incidents as the basis for this report for various reasons, of course, again. But, still, these are the same victims from the incidents, largely, if not 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So your Sarajevo Six samples encompasses the Centar municipality, Ilidza, Novi Grad, Novo Sarajevo, Stari Grad, and Vogosca. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And everywhere in your Sarajevo Six sample, you count all the deaths for which you have a record which occurred on these territories during the indictment period?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Sarajevo Six area, in the indictment period, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Defence counsel is asking whether you count all, all the deaths. Are we talking about all the deaths or the war-related deaths?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, my assumption is that we all realised that we are talking about violent, war-related deaths, right? So I'm not interested in natural deaths, obviously, because we are speaking of a conflict situation. So I assumption is that we all understand what we are talking about; the statistics relevant to this case, to this indictment. It cannot be about natural death. There is not what are you talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So in order to include the data in your Sarajevo Six sample during the Dragomir Milosevic indictment period, you have made no distinction between deaths occurred on the territory of the Ilidza which was controlled by the BH army, and the death occurred on the territory of the municipality controlled by the Republika Srpska army. You have not made that distinction. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So for things to be clear for the record, you have not made this distinction?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not made this distinction because I wasn't able to use data on incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And this was my very point, has been so since the very beginning. Excuse me. Now, as regards the methods you used for the estimates used in your expert report, I invite -- or I ask everyone to look at Table 2 on page 15 of the expert report, and I would like to discuss that briefly. In order to prepare that Table, you have used the statistical data pertaining to ten Sarajevo municipalities between 1989 and 1991. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct to state that these are the deaths occurred in peacetime in these municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And for the purposes of your report, you calculated a yearly average of deaths for this Sarajevo Ten sample pertaining to those years. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Next, you multiplied this by four; in other words, you multiplied the average by four to calculate a death estimate in the absence of conflict or war in these municipalities. I don't know how you reached that figure because my result was 14.168 and you obtained 14.167. Is this a typo or are we talking about the special statistical methods you have to subtract one? Could you explain this or perhaps there is just a typo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is rather a rounding error, or something like that. The computer did it, simply.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you look at the next page. On that page, you look at the number of deaths extracted from your sources after removing the double entries, which is 26.466. You subtracted 14.168 and you reached the number of 12.298. What is stated in the report is 12.299, but we have agreed on that figure. So the figure should have been 12.299 deaths which can be related to war. This is an estimate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a very rough estimate, if, based on the assumption, if the number of natural deaths would be the same as on average before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that any statistical method when it is based on the future; that is, the numbers of death which has not occurred yet are based on -- or is based on hypothesis, on assumptions?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, making predictions involves making assumptions, and some observed data as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, could you please take the previous page again, Table 2. You haven't done that in your expert report, but this is something I did. What I have done is calculate an average of deaths for your Sarajevo Six sample. Let us check this together. Let us check my calculation together and the method that I used. I have taken the figure of 2.372, to which I added 1.056 for Ilidza, 1.836 for Novi Grad, 2.040 for Novo Sarajevo. I added 1.343 for Stari Grad, and 402 finally for Vogosca. I obtained 9.049 deaths. And we're talking about the number of deaths for three years; that is, 1989 to 1991, divided by three, and I obtained 3.013. So that would be the yearly average for the Sarajevo Six sample. It is an estimate for that sample of the yearly number of deaths. Do you agree that this is the total of the average of total death, both natural and violent, but in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you are just redoing this for the Sarajevo Six area, but what's your point? I think these numbers were provided in my report for contextual purposes, and I didn't attach any meaning to them and explain these in the report. The reason for this is that the population of Sarajevo, and not only of Sarajevo of Bosnia and Herzegovina, moved a lot during the conflict. There were huge migrations, internal and international, so this number is highly hypothetical that I presented. So it is just, you know, like a frame. What if there was no conflict, but the conflict was there. So practical meaning is nothing of this -- of very rough estimates.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You have been talking migration among the population of Sarajevo Ten and Sarajevo Ten --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Six.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But can we assume that those who emigrated were younger because they were more able to travel? Is this a safe assumption?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That might be, but I don't think I would like to comment on migration from and into Sarajevo because I didn't study this in this report. Generally, I think it is a very difficult issue to study due to lack of proper information about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you have not studied the matter. Still, you used it to discard the estimate method in your report, and this is the reason why you favoured the so-called extrapolation method. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand what you are saying. You are saying that I used it to discard the estimate method in my report. What estimate method? The rough estimate I presented in Table 2?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if it is the rough estimate or not. But you have stated yourself that this method is used frequently, and you have used it yourself to establish the number of deaths which are war-related. So this figure is the right one, approximately, is it not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you are right. I presented this rough estimate for contextual purposes. It is important to understand what was the scale of mortality in Sarajevo before the conflict in order to have a better perspective on the scale of conflict victimisation, and that is the only purpose I produced; and as such, it is, in my view, justified to have this figure. But I did not produce this figure, this roughly estimate, as an estimate of -- as a basis for the other estimate of war-related deaths in my report. This was not the intention, and there is nothing like this in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. That is why I put the question to you. Why is it not included in your report? Why had you rather used the extrapolation method? You attributed all deaths, some of which are not war-related. Why did you attribute all these deaths to the war?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think I can agree that I used extrapolation method. I used counting approach, counting approach on the first place. These are the absolute minimum numbers of the killed persons that are presented in this report as the major statistics. I also produced more likely minimum numbers. More likely minimum numbers involved, in part, the number obtained from the counting approach; and in the second part, an estimate which is no more just -- than just redistribution of deaths from unknown causes, reported under unknown causes. Well, you call it an extrapolation approach. I call it an adjustment. It not even an extrapolation; it is an adjustment. And I still believe that it is a far better method, a far better method than any rough estimate, other estimate presented by anybody, including myself here in this report. It is just the best one can do in certain situations. And regarding causes of death, you also said something about causes of death. I think you were referring to the unknown causes. Indeed, there is a number of records reported under unknown causes, and there is very little we can do about it. The best we can do is we can redistribute them into natural and violent war-related causes, using the redistribution between the two. This is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, precisely. The method which you mention at the beginning of your report, did this method help you in carrying out your work in redistributing the number of deaths and recording the unknown causes of death based on the data that was provided to you by the statistical institutes to avoid artificially increasing these numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question actually?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Let me give you an example, and let's go to page 22 of your report. We have a chart here before us, and this is Figure 7a. This is Sarajevo Ten sample, and the period covered is a four-year period. You remember, I'm sure, we have here 12.298. This is a number of deaths. According to your estimation method, this could be attributed to war-related deaths. Do you remember this? A while ago, we mentioned this on page 16. The figure you came up with when you deducted it from the figure 26.466 and 14.168. By computing the mean average per annum, the years without a war over a period of four years, the figure obtained is 12.298. So in comparing this figure with the one you provided when analysing your sources, according to you, these were reliable data, total number of deaths 12.003; and then deaths through natural causes, 9.588 and 400.868 [as interpreted]. Does this ring a bell when you see that the estimates, the data provided is data stemming from the death certificates?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The figure is 4.868, not 400.868.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another figure is --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We shall get back to other figures. I would like to you answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that this figure from Table 7a and the other table, Table 2, was it are very similar? Is this what you are saying? So they have very similar. Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, after that, you apply your method. You call it a counting method, which is closer to extrapolation. So it is a very complicated for people like me, lawyers like me. So you then come up with a figure which is 14.199; and when you compare this with the figure obtained by applying the estimation method; in order words, the number of deaths which are not war related, if that figure had remained the same, proportionally speaking, in other words, throughout the period 1989/1991, the figure should have been 12.298. These should be war-relate the deaths. So, according to the sources, this figure is 12.013; and after the adjustment you made, according to the counting method, as you call it, you then have the figure of -- the figure of 14.199. What about these differences? As a demographer, what do you may of these differences?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, as I said, these numbers you discussed based on Table 2 were presented in my report for contextual purposes, and it really doesn't matter that these numbers are as they are; and next to them, there are other statistics present in the report. Well, the difference between the first set of rough estimates and the major statistics is that about the first ones, we don't know anything, but the assumptions that were used to produce them. That's all we know about them. About the major statistics that are presented in the my report, we know much more than that. You know the sources; you know how good they were; how large they were; you know who made them; you know that the sources were unbiased because all ethnic groups are represented in establishing of the sources; you know the causes of death; you know the military status, how was it reported; you know the deficiencies, including among others, the number of unknown causes of death reported in the databases. So what I'm trying to say is it does matter. It really does matter what we know about the statistics that are presented as the major.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I must admit that I have understood nothing. My question was a very simple one. As a demographer and a scientist, what do you make of this? Don't you think this raises questions when you see that, on the one hand, you have reliable sources, even if in certain cases the deaths are due to unknown causes, and the estimates get close. Didn't this lead you to distribute this figure differently, these 4.868 deaths on line 8 of your chart as a sum total of deaths due to unknown causes. Do you know because you proceeded differently? I just need to move on to my next question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You spoke for some time, Ms. Isailovic, but you didn't ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, Your Honour..

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I asked the question: As a scientist, did Mrs. Tabeau -- on seeing these figures, did she not want to redistribute them differently so that these figures -- so the figures could be more in line with the estimates, estimates which would have been provided had the war not occurred?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is your answer to that, Mrs. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The estimates presented in Table 2 were meant to provide a contextual situation. These are figures that should not be seen as figures relating to this indictment. The statistics I produced for this indictment are those discussed yesterday in terms of concrete numbers, and they are mentioned in executive summary and of course throughout the report. And in relation to the distribution or, say, redistribution of the deaths number of deaths of unknown causes, I applied the statistical approach. There is a statistical foundation. There is a method for this. There are no subjective assumptions involved. The matter is described in annex number 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could the witness be permit to the finish, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- annex number 4 to this report. I'm not going to into the deaths again. It is the way it should be done. It has been done the good way, and I'm not going to do anything else with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: She's quite happy with what she has done.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I assumed you would say. So you do not come up with an estimate for the 16-month period, August 1994/November 1995, the period covered by the indictment in Sarajevo for the sample Sarajevo Ten. This is not something that you concluded in your report, is it? This only covered the four years of conflict; is that right.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I shall put the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Tabeau, you made an estimate and you came up with a figure of 12.298 which, according to your estimate, were war-related deaths for this sample Sarajevo Ten. This covered the four years of the war. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not right. This is a table, again, presented for contextual purposes. It is the entire conflict period. It is Table 7a a that you are referring to. But there is another table for the Sarajevo Ten, Table 8, in which statistics for August 1994 to November 1995 are included. The table 8, 8a and b are on page 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, this is in your report. I'd like you to turn to page 16. If now you state the contrary, you did come up with an estimate, and this we addressed a while ago. In the first paragraph, "assuming that our total," then you continue by saying that this figure is biased because of migrations. You did not have data provided to you pertaining to these migrations, did you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess you are back with the figure 12.299 mentioned in the first paragraph on page 16. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't have migration available, information about migration available, but I still don't understand why this figure is so important to you, as it really is much boarder than the indictment period that is just -- you know, we are in section 3. If you look at the table of contents, section 3 is about overview of the merged sources on killed persons, and is much boarder than what is really essential for this case and this indictment. It is a discussion of sources and of how we were doing things at different stages of our work and the results obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. I think you should take the break, Ms. Isailovic, to consider that answer. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you have 16 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall therefore right away ask you for an extra ten minutes that I can finish the summary, which I'm about to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Another ten minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let us see how you make do with the 16 minutes and we'll decide. Try to do as much as possible. I myself don't believe that more time is required for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will finish off with this. You did not compute the number of deaths for this sample, Sarajevo Ten, over a period of 16 months, as the period covered by the indictment against Dragomir Milosevic in your report.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned, before the break, Table 8a and b on page 23, and in this table there are statistics for Sarajevo Ten for August 1994/November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you did not compare the figure in this Figure 8a, 1.692, which according to your most reliable sources would be the total number of death -- of violent death, with a figure which would have stemmed from the estimate found in Figure 2. You did not compare these two figures, did you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't do it for your sample Sarajevo Six either, did you, for the period that covers the indictment?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like now to turn to page 5 of your report. These are your findings, the summary of your work as an expert. The last paragraph is the one I'm interested in. You say: "[In English] The above findings suggest that the civilian population of Sarajevo had systematically been the target for military attacks disregarding the actual presence of heavy combat activities. This also indicates that a targeted terror campaign against civilians likely continued for most of the period from August 1994 to November 1995." [Interpretation] These are your findings which we discussed yesterday. I'm sure you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the findings, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We discussed these yesterday, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We asked you several questions about that, and we looked at Figure 8, Figure 11 to be found on page 39 of your report. Let's have a look at this together. Can you confirm that this is a chart that we looked at yesterday, which formed the basis of the findings I have just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Figure 11 is just one of several findings, based on which this conclusion was drawn. And, indeed, it was presented yesterday as slide number 8, in addition to the presentation in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now ask the usher to blow up this figure as much as possible. It is now more legible on the screen than it is on paper, because we have various colours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, now, the figures you used were the ones which you obtained by the method we mentioned a while ago to establish or to prepare this chart. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not right if you mean the method extrapolation. This is a figure that is obtained based on absolute minimum numbers, from which deaths of unknown causes are excluded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, you have used the figures which are to be found on Figure 8a before adding all of this up; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Sarajevo Six, so respective tables for Sarajevo Six.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So Figure 9a, which you can find on page 17, and you did not include ... Are you with me? This is Figure 9a.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it is Figure 9. Oh, yes, you are right. Figure 9 which is repeated in section 4 where I discuss the major statistics, as Table 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: We need to look at 9a. This is on page 17.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: To begin with, in this case, as far as Figure 11 is concerned, you used the data which you can find in Figure 9a, but you did not include the figure for 1.097 deaths who died of unknown cause; in other words, it was not determined whether this was a natural or violent death?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. And, of course, yes. This is what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On Figure 11, which we are about to discuss, you factored in 981 deaths, violent cause of death cases. After that, you redistributed this between the soldiers and civilians; in other words, you came up with a figure of 419 soldiers and 499 civilians; is that right. 449 civilians.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: 449 civilians, that's correct, and 419 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So the 113 of unknown status, we don't -- they were a part of the military and are not included in Figure 11; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. They are left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: With that said, let's turn to page 39 and Figure 11. We have in the ratio of dead civilians and dead soldiers, this formed the -- the basis of part of your findings, which I read out to you a few moments ago. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this figure, we have the ratio of civilians killed and soldiers killed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to turn to ratio 11, which pertains to the month of January, 1995. This is one of the most striking features of this chart. This was, according to your findings, a period which was a quiet period, and the red represents the civilians. In January, there was -- in January, there were 11 civilians killed and one soldier, is that right, which is why we have this ratio here, which is the ratio of 11?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to recall what was said about municipalities a while ago. Now, in red, we have here the 11 civilians pertaining to the month of January. These were deaths that had occurred in a part of the municipality that was part of Sarajevo Six. This was Ilidza, which was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ilidza is part of Sarajevo Six and partly was controlled by Republika Srpska, partly by the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So, as we don't know, but there is a likelihood that these 11 deaths, who died a violent death, these deaths occurred in part of the municipality of Ilidza that was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska. Therefore, these deaths cannot necessarily be attributed to the accused, who is tried before this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I think, once again, the role of the witness and the role of the Prosecutor need to be clarified. We certainly might make submissions along these lines, based upon this evidence, but I think it is wrong to say that this witness is attributing these deaths to anyone. She is presenting evidence of numbers of violent, war-related deaths which both parties, in conjunction with all of the other evidence in the case, may make such submissions as are logically and factually supported by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what I said to her earlier. That is a matter on which the Prosecutor may make submissions, and indeed in which she may make submissions at the end. But this is not the appropriate witness to put this kind of question to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, perhaps I should develop the point a little more. Yesterday, the Prosecutor had put questions to the witness in relation to the statistics showing a targeted terror campaign against civilians, and you have cross-examined on that matter. I allowed the question because I said ultimately it would be a matter for the Trial Chamber to determine what weight we attach to that kind of evidence. Although I wasn't here yesterday for the last session, I have brought myself up to date, and nothing that I have heard has removed the first impression that I had of this kind of evidence, which is that I would attach no weight to that kind of evidence. As far as the question of the targeting of civilians is concerned, I will have to be persuaded by other evidence than this witness's statistical report and the conclusions on that, and that is also the view of my other colleagues. You can virtually, in fact, you can neglect or set aside that part of the report in which the witness gives a conclusion on the basis of statistical data as to the specific targeting of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber is also aware and acknowledges that the Figure 11 does not give any indication as to who was the perpetrator. So let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. In that case, that will definitely shorten my cross-examination. This was what I wanted to hear about from the Chamber. Now, let me conclude.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as this figure is concerned, the figure which is included in the report, as Mrs. Tabeau is a serious scientist, there's just one answer I would like to elicit. As far as the red part of this figure is concerned, of this diagram, can you confirm that on looking at this chart, we don't know which side of the municipality we're talking about, as the confrontation line crossed these municipalities. We don't know on which side the victims were.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that they had for entire municipalities included, Sarajevo Six municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you didn't factor in the fact that over the period covered by the indictment, these municipalities, with the exception of Stari Grad perhaps, that there was a dividing line between the warring factions here?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, there is with an a confrontation line located around Sarajevo up on the hills. But if you realise that the population of Sarajevo was concentrated in the very heart of the city, then you realise that almost the entire population of the urban part of Sarajevo, Sarajevo Six, lived within the confrontation lines. So even though we, in statistical terms, used administrative units, that means entire municipalities, in terms of the population where they lived, we cover by the study mainly the population that was staying within the confrontation lines. From this point of view, it is a very good approximation of the indictment area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you had no proof about what you are stating today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the concentration of the population? Oh, I think I could provide the proof. We studied the population of Sarajevo based on nijetsa sjednica [phoen] in our previous project in the Galic project, in which I also made an expert report; and then we made the effort to approximate the population living within the front lines, and that is one of the conclusions from that study. So I have a proof, although it is not directly presented in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you are saying that if we were to take the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, which Grbavica belonged to, that Grbavica was not inhabited by civilians? Is that the main thrust of what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not what I said. I said the population was concentrated on a smaller area than the geographic area of the six municipalities; geographic area of the six municipalities, in terms of administrative units, right? So it is not that the population there in that city was uniform and spread over the entire area of every municipality. Population density was much higher in the heart of the city than in the suburbs, and this is what I'm saying that is there is an experience I have from my previous work based on which I am saying this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, I shall conclude. The civilian population killed during the war in Grbavica, which was part of the Novo Sarajevo municipality, is shown in red in Figure 11; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: If Grbavica was part of that administrative unit called Novo Sarajevo, then civilians from this municipality killed during the conflict from August 1994 to November 1995 are shown red.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Were you given proof of the fact that Grbavica was controlled by the army of the Republika Srpska for the purpose of your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention to what army controlled what areas. It was beyond this report, at least beyond the interest I had in this particular report. The purpose was to produce statistics that would cover the indictment period and indictment area as closely as I can get, and this is what I did. For instance, if I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sorry. I think you have answered enough. Let us bring this to an end now, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was my last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Briefly, Your Honour. But before I begin, could Mr. Whiting and I have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Only a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I want to re-examine the witness on one fairly specific point only. With all respect, Your Honour, I also feel that I would be derelict in my duty if I did not note for the record the Prosecution's objection to the ruling made by the Trial Chamber concerning the weight to be given to this witness's evidence. I trust that the Chamber will, when submissions are made at the end of the case, be willing to listen to what the Prosecution has to say to evaluate this evidence, in the light of all the other evidence that has been received in the case. I, of course, acknowledge and accept that it is for the Chamber to assign weight, but I'm simply noting for the record that we are trusting that the Chamber will, of course, keep an open mind and look at all of this evidence as a whole when we make our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And we take note of your submissions, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, just one question, and it concerns something that you and Ms. Isailovic were discussing at the very beginning of cross-examination when a number of questions were asked about the sources that you used. Do you remember the discussion that I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember the discussion in general. I don't know which part specifically you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, I'm about to help you with that. There were questions concerning coverage of the sources, and I believe your evidence was that the sources did have some gaps in coverage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then my question would be: As a result of this deficiency, would the numbers in your report, as a result of this, be lower than otherwise, higher than otherwise, or would this not have an affect on those numbers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These numbers certainly are lower than otherwise. My numbers are just minimum numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Ms. Isailovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Mr. Docherty and Dr. Tabeau kindly slow down, please, because it is extremely difficult to listen. If it goes too fast, the interpreters can't do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will ask you to speak slow and observe the pause between question and answer. I ask the witness and Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That actually concluded my redirect, Your Honour. Does any part of it need to be repeated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well let us hear, Ms. Isailovic. Are you content with that? He is now finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you like, I will read the transcript afterwards, but it is rather unpleasant when there is no pause between question and answer. It is difficult to follow, but I will check the transcript afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, afterwards may be too late. If you have an objection to make, for example, now is the time to make it, but I take it that you have none.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Can I put -- I would like to put the question again. It was short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, put the question again then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mrs. Tabeau, my question is: Do the gaps in coverage of your sources cause the numbers in your report to be higher than otherwise, lower than otherwise, or do they not affect -- do the gaps in coverage not affect the numbers in your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gaps, of course, had a considerable impact on statistics which are lower than otherwise. If there were no gaps, the statistics would be more complete and simply higher than what we were able to produce; not only the gaps, but also other reasons are that the statistics are that low. For instance, a number of records of war-related violent deaths were rejected because of deficiencies. It is that we require a certain standard for a record to be included as part of or statistics. If the standard was not kept, the record was excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tabeau. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And witness number 75 is Mr. Barry Hogan. No, I meant the 75th witness to give evidence. I have been numbering them that way. It is number 76 actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my colleague Mr. Waespi will take the next and final witness for the Prosecution. May I be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. And you may begin, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness Hogan.

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you please state for the record your full name?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Barry Alan Hogan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I take you are an employee of the OTP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And four how long have you been an employee?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: I first joined the Tribunal in October 1998, but I left in October 2004. I rejoined in March 2006, and I have been employed since 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, very briefly, your background before you joined the OTP for the first time.

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: I was a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police from 1975 until I joined the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: While in OTP, were there specific cases you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: When I first joined, I was assigned to the Bosnian Serb leadership case. In spring of 1999, I was reassigned to investigate events in Kosovo.
