I was working in the refugee camps in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia for a number of months, and then I went to the western part of Kosovo as a liaison officer/investigator until approximately November of 1999. When I returned to The Hague, I was reassigned to the Stanislav Galic case, siege of Sarajevo case in January 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were you also assigned to a field office outside The Hague while working for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was. In June of 2003, I was reassigned to the Banja Luka field office in Republika Srpska, and I remained there until October 2004 when I left the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As part of your duties, as you just described, were you involved in efforts to locate the documents or the document archive of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I made repeated efforts to locate the those archives, obtain documents relating to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, both during the investigation of the Stanislav Galic case and while I was at the field office in Banja Luka. All those attempts were negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you very briefly describe those attempts, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: In the OTP, we have a procedure that has been worked out with the governments of countries and the entities within the Bosnia-Herzegovina State of requests for assistance. A formal request is prepared, signed either by the chief of Prosecutions or the Prosecutor herself -- I'm sorry. The chief of investigations or the Prosecutor, and forwarded to the governments through embassies or liaison officer. I made a number of such requests for assistance to Republika Srpska, to Bosnia-Herzegovina federation, to the government of Serbia, and I was unsuccessful in getting any positive replies. I was always told that the archives were not available. Their locations were unknown, and they were not able to comply with our requests. While I was at the field office in Banja Luka, I had many meetings with government officials including the Prime Minister, Minister of Interior, the Chief of the army of Republika Srpska, and again made repeated requests for not only the collection of documents from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, but from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and the Presidency archives. All three of these collections had been subject of repeated requests over the years, and none of the archives had been made available to the OTP. It got to the point where the Prosecutor herself during meetings in Banja Luka insisted that criminal investigations be conducted by the authorities of the Republika Srpska into the theft of state-owned archives; and as liaison officer at the field office, I was recipient of updates on the progress of those investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I understand that despite what you said, that these efforts were fruitless, in the end they were successful because you have had access to the archive documents of the SRK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when did you have access to the archive?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: We had -- I had access to the archives in June of -- I'm sorry, in May of 2006 as a result of a further follow-up request for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what do these archives contain, as you found out in May 2006?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: They contain the collection of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps documents from the army of Republika Srpska, the Main Staff archive collection from the army of Republika Srpska plus a number of different corps, such as some Drina corps documents, Herzegovina corps documents, and I don't believe I saw any Krajina corps documents there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where are these archives located, the ones that you saw in May 2006 for the first time and that contained the documents you just described?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: They're contained in a basement wing of the Kozara barracks, which is an army facility in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Trial Chamber the -- how it was set up, the way access an organised, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: The access to the archives was only granted to me and my colleagues from the OTP with prior written permission of the Ministry of Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The archives itself, as I say, were a basement wing. There is a locked, steel door separating that archive location from the rest of the building. The military building in which the archives are contained have uniformed soldiers guarding the entrance, various offices within that building, and the barracks building itself is on an army base which is fenced, guarded by uniformed soldiers and access a controlled by those uniformed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: When you visited the archive for the first time in May 2006, did you have contact with the archivist?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I met with Captain Sindrak, as well as some other officers, but I was told that Captain Sindrak was in charge of the physical facilities there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did he relay any information to you in relation to the origins and the source of the documents he was now in charge of?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, he did. During that meeting and during subsequent meetings and conversations, I learned from Captain Sindrak that military reforms had been under way in Bosnia-Herzegovina since late 2004; and in earlier 2006, the armies of the Republika Srpska and the federation had been amalgamated into one army at the state level. As part of the military reforms, orders had been issued by the entity armies, late in 2004, that all documents and archive material should be forwarded to central locations. I was told that in the case of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps documents and other Republika Srpska army documents, orders had been issued to all existing military facilities and barracks to send all of their documents to Banja Luka to the Kozara barracks. Captain Sindrak told me that in the case of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps documents, they had been received at the end of November, early December 2004 from a military barracks in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Subsequent to your first visit in May 2006 to these archives in Banja Luka, were you part of another mission that actually went into the archives and looked at the documents themselves for the purpose of obtaining evidence for the OTP.

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was the mission leader of a mission at the end of June, early July 2006, and we did research and collected a number of documents, scanned a number of documents from those archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How many people were involved in that mission you were the leader of?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: There were 12, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how was it organised? Can you very briefly tell us how these documents were processed?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Besides this particular case, there were other cases for which we were doing research during that mission. We had two military analysts. We had one attorney from another team and two members of the Prosecution team for this case doing research. We also had language assistants. We had two staff members from the evidence unit to scan the documents, and we had an analyst to track the documents which we were scanning and to prepare a spreadsheet of the documents that were being collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You talk about scanning documents. Did you see the originals of these documents?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how do you know these were originals?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: The vast majority of the documents that I saw were signed and/or stamped in ink other than the colour of the typed document; in other words, it appeared to be original signatures, original stamps with handwritten notes. Many documents were typewritten, and you could see the impressions of the type face on the document itself. There were carbon copies, which were typical carbon paper with an obvious carbon impression on the paper. There were also telexes which were on different coloured paper than the rest of the documents. I describe it as tan-coloured paper that comes in a roll, and then it as -- as a document is being printed on the electronic transmission, the paper is torn off from the roll so that sometimes the document ends up being twice as long as a normal A4 size, sometimes half as short as a A4 size.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where are the originals today of the documents we are about to show to Your Honours, to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: All the originals are still in the archives in Banja Luka at the Kozara barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you have any information whether the Defence in this case had a chance to see the archives as well?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: I was told by Captain Sindrak that Mr. Tapuskovic, in particular, had already visited the archives in March of 2006, and that he or any other Defence attorney was free to do any research there with the permission of the Ministry of Defence. The same rules applied to the OTP. We were free to do additional research at the archives with the permission of the Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, if the 65 ter number 03128, page 4 to 12, could be brought up. We do have, Mr. President, a hard copy binder of these 85 documents which might assist you. It's also prefaced by the spreadsheet which has relevant information about all these 85 documents, but I intend to lead the witness electronically through three examples so we can look there e-court. It might be easier for you, Mr. President, to have it aside. It's both in original B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to have it. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just a question because on my list I have 82 documents. Are we talking about 85 documents or 82 documents, because I counted myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: According to my information, we have 85 documents. Perhaps we can figure out the right number as we go along.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could have a look at the spreadsheet which is now in front of you on the screen, can you tell Their Honours what this spreadsheet represents?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: This spreadsheet is a list of a selection of documents which were scanned at the Kozara barracks archives of the former army of Republika Srpska during my mission in June and July 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what it represents, what the information contained in this spreadsheet is about? I can confirm, thanking my colleague, that it is indeed 82 documents and not 85.

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: The first column, of course, is 65 ter number. The second column is the author of the -- the author's name as it appears on the document; then comes the date of the document. The fourth column is a comment that was created by one of our military analysts and myself. The next two columns, of course, are the evidence reference numbers. The column which is labeled "relevance" is again authored by one of our military analysts with some input from myself, showing what we believe this document will be able to tell the Court. And the final column is the number of paragraph of the indictment to which this document refers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hogan. Let me ask you first: Did you look at all these 82 documents yourself?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could have a look at three examples. The first one is in your binder, Your Honours, tab 11, which represents 65 ter number 02016.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If that could be brought up, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Hogan, can you talk a little bit about this document, about the authenticity as it appeared to you at the time and today.

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a -- what I call a telex. It might not have been an actual telex machine that transported this document; however, I refer to telex as any form of electronic transmission. It was, as far as I recall, on the brownish or tan-coloured paper amongst other original documents in the archives in one of the binders. It has the signature block of Major-General Dragomir Milosevic; however, it is it unsigned because it was an electronic transmission. At the top of the document, you can see the handwriting for BVP or 4th Battalion of military police, and the word "vratiti" which I believe was translated as return or reply. That would have been in handwritten ink on that original document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, I have something different in tab 11. I don't know in I'm out of place somewhere, but could you help us identify the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I'm guessing it might be in your version tab 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It is. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hogan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we move on to the next document, which will be ter number 02182, and that should be in my tab 19, but that appears to be, Your Honours, tab 21. It's a document dated 2nd January 1995. Yes, that's the document that appears now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Hogan, can you tell Their Honours about your impression of what this -- the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Again, this document was found in one of the binders amongst other original documents. This one has the signature block of Major-General Dragomir Milosevic, as well as his handwritten signature. It has the stamp of the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. It has a transmission receipt stamp, bottom right, with handwritten notes, and a --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to make everybody's work easier, I have given this to Dragomir Milosevic. The Defence does not challenge the authenticity of these documents. Just to avoid this. I'm only worried about this difference because I provided a binder to Mr. Milosevic, and I want to be quite sure that we're talking about the same binder, the same binder that the Bench has.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It is the same binder. I just wanted to show Their Honours and to everyone three samples of these documents, and I'm happy to hear that the Defence doesn't object to its admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you have anything more to add to this document; if not, we will move on to the last example, which is ter number 02197, which is very likely in tab number 24. And while that is being retrieved, Mr. Hogan, how many documents were there in the collection you have looked at in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: There were tens of thousands of documents in the collection of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and further tens of thousands of documents in the Main Staff collection. From the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I believe we selected 3.300, it could be 3.370, documents to scan and enter into evidence; plus, the original maps and ledgers that we brought back for scanning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you see any gaps in the sequence of documents you have encountered there?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes. There were obvious gaps. There were -- the numbers of the orders should have been subsequently. The dates should have been subsequential. There were obviously documents missing from various binders, various collections. I did speak to the archivist, Captain Sindrak, about this, and he was able to tell me that everything that was sent to them at the archives was contained in the binders that we were examining. They were not saving anything back; however, it was obvious to him that there had been documents removed from the total collection, prior to it arriving at the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hogan. A very brief comment on the document that you see on the screen.?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document that was -- originated at the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade. It has the original stamp and handwritten notation at the top left, and it has the signature and stamp of the 3rd -- sorry, the signature, I believe, is Dragan Jusipovic. It is also written in Cyrillic so it is harder to decipher, but it has the stamp of the command of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade at the back. I think this was one of the typewritten documents because you can see obvious strike-overs at various places within the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hogan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender the spreadsheet we discussed a moment ago, which is ter number 03128; and, second, all 82 documents and they should receive individual numbers, and I understand that can be done outside the courtroom. And my case manager just tells me that the documents we just discussed, the three, are already exhibits, and I can give the exhibit numbers to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, can we confirm that all of these 82 documents were collected by Mr. Hogan in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Hogan, can you answer Judge Harhoff's question?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, all 82 of these documents were collect the on the mission that I led in June and July of 2006. I cannot confirm that I selected each and every one of those documents; but if I did not do it personally, then somebody on my mission did, and they were scanned all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And they were all taken from the archives.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, on what basis do you say these documents are admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, as the rule requires, Rule 89, they are relevant; and you see in the last column of your spreadsheet, a list in relation to each document what the relevance is. It goes command and control; it goes to the subordinate unit; it is goes to the disciplinary action, which was instituted by the accused. And that's been done for each single document. Second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, of course, we haven't seen the documents themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. But I can -- Mr. President, I can go through each document, but it's all listed for each document. Of these 82 documents, there is a separate column about relevancy. You have in your binder each document, so you can compare each document as it relates to the indictment. You can look at the comments made by Mr. Hogan and our military expert, and they explain the relevancy of each of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have done something like this before?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, Witness Nakas was a witness who introduced medical records which were not all signed by him but by other parts, and he talked about authenticity of these records. The authenticity, Mr. President, Your Honours, I think has been several laid by Witness Hogan, and the Defence didn't object to really a limited amount of documents, 82 out of thousands of relevant documents. We have carefully selected these documents, and I think that they are all very, very helpful for Your Honours' determination about the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It seems to be the practice of the Prosecution to bring in cases as a last witness a kind of wrap-up witness who puts in all these documents. In the other Milosevic case that I was involved in, I remember we had this experience. We went through the documents, I believe, and looked at those that were public documents and admitted them. Part of the problem is that the practice in Trial Chambers is not consistent in these matters. I think some Chambers will admit, others will not, and maybe it is the bulk of the documentation here. But as a matter of principle, I suppose the bulk should not make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I accept that Mr. President, and we have looked at other cases. For instance, the Martic case introduced more documents in our case; namely, 149 documents that came in with investigator, Ari Kerkkanen, an OTP analyst. In the Milutinovic case, Phil Coo brought in documents and there were other cases. Indeed, Mr. President, it is important in these cases, as you are well aware. Military accused who issued directives, orders, I think that is important for to see relevant documents, which show the issues that are at stake. His exercise of command and control. His ability to initiate disciplinary proceedings. This is all very, very relevant, and there is no other way to introduce these documents, these very limited number of documents. I'm sure, if you read them and go through each of them, you will find them very helpful. They are very short. Most of them are just one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, in your jurisdiction, these documents would not be admitted in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I don't think that is it correct. I think they would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour,. They have been properly authenticated by a witness. They are essentially business records that are stored in an archive, and the basis that the witness has given is certainly sufficiently reliable to -- for authenticity to be established so that the court can make that finding and rely on them. They are relevant, and they are probative. We have made a substantial showing of authenticity. The Defence does not object to their admission. Compared to other cases, it is a small number of documents, only 82. We did canvass a number of other cases, and I can give additional examples to the ones given by Mr. Waespi. We found approximately ten examples of other cases where document collections were admitted into evidence. For all those reasons, this would be, in my submission, admitted in my jurisdiction. Certainly, the rules of admission are more lenient, for obvious reasons, here in this Tribunal than in typical common law jurisdiction, because it is a -- because Your Honours are -- will be able to assign the appropriate weight to the documents at a later time. For that reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was merely being curious because we are not operating in a common law jurisdiction here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, just as a matter of curiosity and information, would the documents be admitted in your jurisdiction in this way?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think this was always a problem with lawyers who are coming from the civil law system; because in our system, an authentic document contains probative value in itself. So, as far as I'm concerned, I find it very difficult to admit that the content of a document should be proven by someone who can only confirm that the fact actually occurred. So from the Serb and French jurisdiction standpoint, I believe that authentic documents carry a lot of weight and, therefore, it's not a question of admitting the documents or not. Documents came from the archives and the archives are properly administered. It is a problem for to us introduce the documents for very selfish reasons. The Defence does not challenge the tendering of these documents. We don't challenge the authenticity of these documents because we know that they come from the archives which are properly administered and according to the law applicable in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Following the law and practice of the Tribunal, in particular Rule 89(C), the Chamber admits the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will admit the spreadsheet, 65 ter 03128, as P639. The additional 82 documents will be assigned exhibit numbers this afternoon, and a memo will be circulated tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have just two or three more questions to the witness in relation to another assignment Mr. Hogan had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Hogan, are you familiar with a spreadsheet summarising Bosnian police investigate reports?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you tell us what these reports were about?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: These reports were a collection of local Sarajevo police investigations into shelling and sniping incidents between August 1994 and November 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please move closer to the microphone thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how many reports did that concern?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: I believe the spreadsheet contained approximately 200, maybe just slightly above 200, but the total collection of reports between 11th of August 1994 and the 30th of November 1995 was 754 such reports of shelling and sniping incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hogan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Mr. Hogan. I think we know each other. I'm one of the lawyers of Mr. Dragomir Milosevic. You are the last witness presented by the Prosecution, and I'm happy to see you but I have no questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. But Judge Mindua has one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I just wanted to the check this with you on the archives. You turned to were the archives in Banja Luka not in Sarajevo. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BARRY HOGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The archives in Banja Luka were the archives of the former army of Republika Srpska. The archives in the Sarajevo are the archives of the former army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Bosniak army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hogan, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for giving it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Prosecutor, is that your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, we have to do a few housekeeping matters before we can rest. I'm not sure what the time of the break is. I have kind of lost track. If you want to do them now or take a break, it could take about ten, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The break would be at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we can get started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first thing we need to do is there were a number of statements that were admitted by the Trial Chamber via Rule 92 bis and 92 quater, and a number of those had to be -- redactions were required. We have done that and they now need to be assigned exhibit numbers, and we could go through that process now. I could give you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. One of them doesn't have a -- I will do the best I can. There may be one or two that we will have to do after the break. The first one is Ismet Alic. His two 92 bis statements were admitted by decision of 27 February 2007 with redactions, which have been done. It is 65 ter 31289, and if that could be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is a purely technical question. In order to be able to check with what I have in my notes, would it be at all possible after the break, or perhaps we could have the break now, so that I would be able to see the document and compare with the rulings you made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is perfectly in order. So that the Defence, which obviously has an interest in this matter, should be able to ascertain that the corrections have been made, the redactions have been made, rather, I think we will take the break now and resume in 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think we're now on the same page with the Defence with respect to the 92 bis and 92 quater witnesses. I will just read them and out, and Mr. Monkhouse has advised me that it would be easiest if I just I read them out and assign numbers to all of them afterwards, the rather than doing one at I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The first one is Ismet Alic. Two statements were admitted via Rule 92 bis with redactions on the 27th of February 2007. The 65 ter number is 312. Then there is Fadila Serdarevic. Two statements, via Rule 92 bis, without redactions, 27 February, 2007, and the 65 ter number is 3135. Zejna Sljivo. One statement admitted, via Rule 92 bis, decision of 27 February, 2007 without redactions. That's 3136, 65 ter number. Fikreta Pacariz: Three statements, via Rule 92 bis, granted admission by decision of 27 February 2007. Two of them with redactions, one without. That's 3133. Edisa Krso: One statements, via 92 Rule bis, granted on the 27th of February, 2007 with redactions. That's 3134. Mehmed Kamber: One statement, without redactions. Decision is the same date, and it's 3130. Ermin Kreco: Two statements admitted by decision of 3 April 2007. One with redactions, one without. That is 65 ter 3132. Avdo Vatric: Two statements admitted via Rule 92 bis on the 3rd of April, 2007 with redactions, and that is 3137. Witness Mesuda Klaric: One statement admitted without redactions on the 3rd of April, 2007, and that is 3131. Zlatko Medjedovic: Three statements admitted via Rule 92 quater on the 19th of April, 2007. Two of the statements with redactions, one without. That is 3138. So if those could all be assigned number. There is one left which is actually an odd case. It is Witness Djula Leka, and his statement was admitted by the Chamber via Rule 92 bis. However, we then tried to do the 92 bis procedure, and there are medical reasons why that was impossible to do. We have filed a motion this morning to transform the admission of his statement via Rule 92 bis into admission via Rule 92 quater under the same terms as before, which the only difference really is that of course there will be no 92 bis procedure that is done. That was filed only this morning. That obviously can't be decided upon. However, I think there is no reason why we can't close our case today with the understanding that if our motion is allowed, that we be allowed to reopen for -- strictly for the purpose of assigning that statement an exhibit number and putting it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's being suggested that we could mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think that would be fine; however, I think we would still have to go through the procedure. I mean, it's merely a technical that we change it from MFI to an exhibit. I apologise. I referred to that witness as a "he," but it is in fact a "she." The 65 ter number of that statement is 3139. For that one, of course, we are not asking for an exhibit number today, unless Your Honours want to make it an MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just make sure we do not forget it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. Of course, that is a good idea. With all the others, we would ask that they be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 3129 becomes P640. 65 ter 3135 becomes P641. 65 ter 3136 becomes P642. 65 ter number 3133 becomes P643. 65 ter number 3134 becomes P644. 65 ter number 3130 becomes P645. 65 ter number 3132 becomes P646. 65 ter number 3137 becomes P647. 65 ter number 3131 becomes P648. 65 ter number 3138 becomes P649. 65 ter number 3139 will be marked for identification as P650.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There are two other matters that Mr. Sachdeva will take up. One having to do with medical documents, and one having to do with a problem which arose with respect to a specific exhibit. So I will let him address Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. President, Your Honours. The Prosecution makes an application pursuant to Rule 89(C) for the admission of ten hospital records that emanate from the Dobrinja hospital. These records relate to persons that we allege were killed or injured in the scheduled incident, shelling incompetence 14; that is, the Dobrinja Simone Bolivar school. Therefore, we would submit that these reports are probative and relevant and within the parameters of Rule 89(C). Just a brief history. You may recall that the Prosecution had witness Zineta Arifagic down to authenticate these records in court. She had expressed concern because she had left the hospital, she would be unable to appropriately authenticate the records. And in response, the Prosecution applied on the 30th of March, 2007 to amend this witness list and substitute Zineta Arifagic for Dr. Hadzir, who was the former director of the hospital. The response from the Defence objected to the substitution of the witness but did not object to the authenticity of the documents. And in Your Honour's decision of the -- I can't recall the exact date of the decision. But on the 23rd of March -- excuse me. In Your Honour's decision, we were denied to change the witness. However, it was noted that the Defence did not object to the authenticity of the records. So, in that regard, we would push for the admission pursuant to the process of tendering them from the bar table. I note that the Tribunal practice has permitted this manner of tendering documents into evidence; most recently the Milutinovic case on the 27th of March, 2007, a decision by the Chamber permitted the tender of documents from the bar table and admitted the document into evidence, provided, of course, the Prosecution can demonstrate the probative value and the relevancy. I also understand that the Defence maintains their lack of objection to the tendering of these ten -- actually seven death certificates and three medical records.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Just for Your Honours' benefit, the decision was the 13th of April, 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we will admit them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, without a 65 ter number, it is difficult to assign exhibit numbers. If we could be provided those 65 ter number numbers, we can assign those exhibit numbers now or we can do it this afternoon and incorporate that into our memo for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I have the numbers. I was just awaiting a decision from the Trial Chamber. 65 ter number is 00119, and there are ten documents in total and the numbers have been assigned 119, letter A to letter J. I understand that they are uploaded in e-court with their corresponding translations.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 00119 A through J will receive the exhibit numbers P651 through P660, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I thought we ended last with P650 MFI, so the next one in line would be P651.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I believe that is what I said; If not, I stand corrected. It would be P651 through P660, respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought I heard you say 61. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next issue is an issue I think that came about during the sort of teething problems that we had the manner of tendering parts of composite exhibits in the beginning of the case, and it relates to an exhibit that I showed Witness 137. It can be found at transcript reference 2451 to 2452 on the 19th of February, 2007, and it concerns Exhibit P252. What I had shown the witness was a technical bomb squad report on the Markale 2 incident, and I had asked for pages 22 to 30 of exhibit -- sorry, 65 ter 891 to be brought up on the screen, where I then proceeded to show the witness four pages from those eight pages; that Is, 22 to 30. Upon the witness confirming the document, I asked for the document to be entered into evidence, and I stated on the record that it should be pages 1 to 4 of 65 ter number 891. What I, in fact, meant was 1 to 4 of the pages 22 to 30; therefore, pages 22 to 25 of the 65 ter 891. I recently had a look at the e-court and the Prosecution exhibit 252 that is uploaded is not the document that I showed the witness and, therefore, I ask your leave to substitute the exhibit to the correct exhibit that was shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the correct exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: The correct exhibit is a technical report by the bomb squad on the Markale incident, and it is pages 22 to 25 of 65 ter 891; the English being 15 to 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have nothing against this. I also have an application to make. I thought Mr. Sachdeva had finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Well, this is not going to be a case of one hand washing the other. We'll admit it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just a few other minor housekeeping matters, if I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next one is, as Your Honours are aware, on the 17th of April, the Prosecution filed a motion seeking certification to appeal a decision of the Trial Chamber with regard to adjudicated facts. The Defence also filed a motion seeking certification, I believe, one or two days before that. We, of course, have not received a decision yet from the Trial Chamber, so I would just ask that we be allowed to close today our case on the condition that if certification is allowed by the Trial Chamber, and if the Prosecution's appeal is successful before the Appeals Chamber, that we then be allowed again to reopen our case in order to admit into evidence whatever additional adjudicated facts the Appeals Chamber might allow. So it's just a technical procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would follow, in any event, because the Appeals Chamber would require it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would think so, but I'm just trying to be careful. Part of a job of a lawyer is to be careful, to make sure that everything is covered. So I just wanted that to be clear on the record. The next matter is that -- I don't think, though, that it prevents us from closing our case or proceeding with the 98 bis argument tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next issue is I just want to confirm that Your Honours received a memorandum from me yesterday, which was also provided to the Defence, with respect to our continued efforts to identify the location of Captain Idriz and also providing information about a Polish UNMO I wanted to interviewed. I just want to make sure that that was, in fact, received by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, could I just ask you whether the Prosecution has tried to contact the captain in Kenya through UN sources; that is to say, through the UNHCR in Nairobi, because that is frequently a more efficient way of getting through.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The answer to that question is no, and I'm not sure about -- we have would have to consider the protocol involved in that, because typically we respect a certain protocol which involves sending an RFA to the government in order to identify where a person is. If there is no problem with the protocol, I would be happy to take up Your Honour's suggestion and pursue that means, as well, to try to identify where this person is. I just wouldn't want to step on any diplomatic toes in doing so. So I will inquire in our office of about the protocol and what is acceptable and what is not in that regard and pursue it, if we are allowed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not, of course, suggesting that we violate the rules of diplomacy rules, but it could be helpful to pursue both tracks in parallel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think anything at this point could help; but as I stated in the memo, I'm afraid that ultimately it may require some more firm action by the Trial Chamber. I think Your Honours carry a much bigger stick than we do. I would suggest that an order from the Trial Chamber or a subpoena or something of that nature would certainly get a lot of attention. In that memo, I inquired whether the Trial Chamber wanted to have available to it the information report regarding the Polish UNMO who was with Captain Hansen on the date of the incident. I don't know if Your Honours have had an opportunity to consider whether you would like that to be provided to Your Honours or not. It has, of course, been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we will consider that, as well as the submission that you made about compulsory order.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. The final matter, Your Honours will recall, is that during a number of cross-examinations, there were Defence exhibits, which were marked for identification, and for -- for two different reasons. One, some were marked for identification because there was not a proper foundation for the document to come into evidence. Others were marked for identification because there was no translation. I'm currently in discussions with the Defence about which ones fall in which categories and which ones can become exhibits. We don't at the moment fully agree. There are four documents at the moment that are -- actually, I think just two that are in dispute. I think this is something that we can resolve between ourselves and get settled, but I just wanted to alert Your Honours that is an outstanding matter with respect to the record as it now stands. There are some documents which have been marked for identification which will slide over into the exhibits category. It may, at some point, require a decision by Your Honours. I hope it doesn't. I hope we can resolve it between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With those matters addressed and the various conditions that I set out about having to reopen the case in various eventualities, we're prepared to close our case and rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Whiting. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just have one question pertaining to the following: These documents that have been marked for identification which we have agreed upon, we both agree, that's the Prosecution and the Defence, that some are marked for identification because there is no translation. We now have the translations of these documents. They have been provided and input in the e-court system. We have sent them to the Bench and to the OTP. We've sent a list of documents. These are four documents which I would like to tender, and I would like them not to be marked for identification but to be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let us have them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D109, D118, D135, and D136 marked for identification, pending translation. We have now been provided with the translations, and the two documents mentioned by Mr. Whiting were documents number D64 and D100. We will be able to check on the transcript and know exactly had a these documents contained. Mr. Tapuskovic had not intended them to be marked for identification - this was a slip of the tongue - because the documents had prior to that been admitted under no conditions whatsoever. But we need to still check this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: D109, D118, D135, and D136 are admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, those exhibits are retain the exhibit numbers listed, and they will just move from MFI to exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will await the results of the discussions between the Prosecution and the Defence. If they cannot be resolved timely, then the Chamber should be informed so that we can make a decision. Are there any other matters? None. We are to resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are to resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.50 p.m.,
